issues.legal_issue: Tenants in pending rent-default suits or appeals could seek the benefit of the newly introduced instalment-payment procedure even after the ordinary application period had expired.
material_facts: An eviction suit for rent default was pending when an amendment introducing an instalment-payment procedure for rent arrears took effect.
The amendment ordinance applied retrospectively to suits and appeals pending when it commenced.
The tenant applied for instalment relief within one month of the ordinance, although more than one month had passed since service of summons.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was entitled to apply for instalment relief, and the application was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17(2A) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, and section 5 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance No. VI of 1967 must be read together. The retrospective provision extended the new benefit to all pending suits and appeals, so the ordinary time limit did not defeat an application filed within one month of the ordinance. Remedial amendments should be construed liberally to give them effect and to avoid rendering a provision otiose. The Court relied on Madhav Rao Scindia v. Union of India, AIR 1971 SC 530, and Dy. Custodian v. Official Receiver, [1965] 1 SCR 220.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction on the ground of the tenant's rent default.
predicates.suit_or_appeal_pending_when_retroactive_: The suit or an appeal in it was pending when the amendment with retrospective effect commenced.
predicates.application_filed_within_month_of_amendm: The tenant applied for the newly available relief within one month after the amendment commenced.

issues.definition: When a rent-default eviction proceeding was pending on commencement of a retrospective amendment and the tenant applied within one month of that commencement, the tenant could seek instalment relief.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who paid arrears as ordered could claim protection from eviction where later rent defaults did not meet the threshold that disqualified the tenant from relief again.
material_facts: The tenant paid the arrears for the period ending in February 1968 in accordance with the court's instalment orders.
The tenant later paid rent late for two months, with those defaults occurring across a period of thirteen months.
The later defaults did not amount to four months of default within a twelve-month period.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was entitled to the protection of section 17(4), and the suit could not be decreed on the ground of rent default.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17(3) and 17(4), including the proviso to section 17(4), must be read together. Section 17(4) bars a possession decree for rent default when the tenant makes the required payments. Its proviso denies relief again only where a tenant who has already obtained relief subsequently defaults for four months within twelve months; a later default below that threshold does not bar renewed relief.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction on the ground of the tenant's rent default.
predicates.tenant_previously_received_rent_default_: The tenant had previously obtained relief from eviction for rent default.
predicates.court_ordered_arrears_paid: The tenant paid the arrears in accordance with the court's directions.
predicates.subsequent_default_below_repeated_relief: The tenant's later rent defaults fell short of the level that would disqualify the tenant from relief again.

issues.definition: A tenant in a rent-default eviction proceeding who has obtained earlier relief, paid the ordered arrears, and later defaulted below the disqualifying threshold remains protected from eviction for rent default.

issues.legal_issue: The direction to strike out a tenant's defence for rent-payment default is discretionary, and the court may condone delay and extend the time for payment when justice and the circumstances of the case warrant it.
material_facts: The tenant paid rent late for two months, with delays of forty-four days and six days.
The defaults concerned belated payments rather than non-payment of the later rent arrears and were considered technical and inconsequential.
The lower courts treated striking out the defence as mandatory.
issues.conclusion: Striking out the defence was not warranted in the circumstances; the court had discretion not to strike it out and could condone the delay or extend the time for payment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(3) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, is directory: its use of “shall” is read as “may,” leaving the court discretion to strike out or retain the defence in light of the circumstances and the interests of justice. That discretion also permits the court to condone default and extend the time for payment or deposit. The Court relied on Govindlal Chhagganlal Patel v. Agricultural Produce Market Committee, Godhra, [1976] 1 SCR 451; Ganesh Prasad Sah Kesari v. Lakshmi Narain Gupta, [1985] 3 SCC 53; Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, [1980] 2 SCR 334; Santosh Mehta v. Om Prakash, [1980] 3 SCR 325; and Ram Murti v. Bhola Nath, [1984] 3 SCR 111.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.tenant_paid_rent_late: The tenant paid rent after the required time.
predicates.delay_was_technical_and_inconsequential: The delay concerned belated payment rather than non-payment and was not serious in the circumstances.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding, where the tenant paid rent late but the delay was technical and inconsequential, the court may retain the defence and may condone the delay or extend the payment time.
